Part 1 of 6

Moving West

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 1: Explain how, why, and where Americans moved west of the Mississippi River during the 1830s and 1840s.

IN MY WORDS: In your own words, who moved west in the 1830s and 1840s, and where did they go?

Reading AManifest Destiny and the Comanche Empire

The idea of a “manifest destiny” implied that the United States had a God-given mission to extend its Christian republic and capitalist civilization from the Atlantic to the Pacific—and beyond.

In 1840, when the massive migration across the Great Plains began, more than 325,000 Indigenous people inhabited the vast area west of the Mississippi River. . . . The Comanche had become the dominant people of the Southwest over the previous century. . . . Their aim was not to control the land itself but the most valuable resources on it—especially bison and horses.

By the mid-1800s, Comanche raiding parties had pushed farther and farther south into northern Mexico and had succeeded in weakening Mexican control in that region. This sequence of events made northern Mexico vulnerable to conquest—and helped pave the way for White American settlers to enter the region.

Word help: manifest destiny = the belief that God wanted the U.S. to spread across the continent · inhabited = lived in · dominant = most powerful · vulnerable to conquest = easy to take over

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 13, “Moving West” (Indigenous Plains Peoples) (p. 516).

Reading BOregon Fever and the Overland Trails

Soon, Oregon Fever swept the nation, “raging like any other contagion,” as a journalist wrote in 1843. . . . For many, the migration across the punishing terrain came to symbolize the mythic American Dream, whereby a determined people risked everything to gain their own land and enjoy prosperity and independence.

Most of the settlers on the Overland Trails traveled in family groups. Oregon-bound wagon trains usually left Missouri in late spring and completed the grueling 2,000-mile trek by winter. . . . The arduous westward journey, usually five to six months long, was full of hardship amid climatic extremes: broiling summers, fierce thunderstorms and tornadoes, and bitterly cold winters. . . . On average, one grave appeared every eighty yards along the overland trails.

Word help: contagion = a disease that spreads · terrain = land · prosperity = having money and success · grueling, arduous = very hard and tiring · trek = long trip

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 13, “Moving West” (Mountains and Oregon Country) (p. 520).

This modern textbook map (Norton Map 13.1) shows the main trails settlers used to cross the West in the 1840s.

Map key: Orange = Oregon Trail · Dark blue = Mormon Trail · Green dashes = California Trail · Purple = Santa Fe Trail · Independence (Missouri) = where many wagon trains started · Labels in the West = places settlers were going (Oregon, California)

Reading CTexas Breaks from Mexico

By 1823, 3,000 Americans (or Texians, also called Anglos because they spoke English) were living in Texas. Most had migrated from southern states and snapped up inexpensive lands in east Texas that boasted the same rich soils as the cotton-growing South. They dreamed of great cotton wealth to be made in Texas—and they forced enslaved people to move with them.

Determined to tighten his grip on the growing American presence in Texas, he imprisoned Stephen Austin for treason in 1834 and sent troops into Texas. He also talked openly about enforcing anti-slavery laws there. . . . By the fall of 1835, Texians resolved to be free of Mexican interference. . . . As sporadic fighting erupted, hundreds of armed volunteers from southern states rushed to assist the 30,000 Texians in the Texas Revolution against a Mexican nation of 7 million people.

Word help: Texians = Americans who moved to Texas · he = Santa Anna, Mexico’s president · treason = turning against your country · resolved = decided · sporadic = on and off

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 13, “Moving West” (American Settlements in Texas; The Texas War for Independence) (p. 525).

Part 2 of 6

The Mexican-American War

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 2: Examine the causes of the Mexican-American War and its impact on national politics.

IN MY WORDS: Why did the United States go to war with Mexico, and what did it win?

Reading DThe Road to War

As the Comanche continued to push deeper into the Republic of Texas, and Texian calls for American protection escalated, the United States finally annexed Texas in 1845. But the Mexican government refused to recognize the loss of its northern province.

On the evening of May 9, President Polk learned that Mexican troops had attacked U.S. soldiers along the Rio Grande. Eleven Americans were killed. The president now had the pretext for war that he had been seeking. . . . Despite such concerns, Congress complied with Polk’s request and authorized the recruitment of 50,000 soldiers.

Most Whigs across the North, including a young Illinois congressman named Abraham Lincoln, also opposed the war, stressing that President Polk had maneuvered the Mexicans into attacking. The United States, many insisted, had no reason for placing its army in the disputed border region between Texas and Mexico.

Word help: annexed = added to the country · pretext = an excuse · complied = went along · maneuvered = tricked or pushed · disputed = argued over

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 13, “Reviewing the Core Objectives” (p. 568). Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 13, “The Mexican-American War” (Opposition to the War) (p. 532).

Reading EThe Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo

By the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo, signed in February 1848, a humiliated Mexico gave up half its entire territory: all of Texas north of the Rio Grande; the territories that would become the states of California, Arizona, New Mexico; and significant parts of Colorado, Utah, Wyoming, and Nevada (Map 13.4).

The treaty guaranteed the 150,000 Indigenous people and the 80,000 Mexicans living in the ceded territories that they could keep their property, receive U.S. citizenship, and retain their Catholic religion. . . . Over time, however, as Americans streamed in, the ruthless among them cheated and killed Mexican-born residents and Native people. . . . Others had their lands confiscated by the Americans.

Word help: humiliated = deeply embarrassed · ceded = given up · retain = keep · confiscated = taken away

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 13, “The Mexican-American War” (The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848)) (p. 536).

Reading FThe War’s Legacies

The Mexican-American War marked the first time that U.S. military forces had defeated and occupied another country. More than 13,000 Americans died in the conflict, 11,550 of them from disease.

As the years passed, however, critics charged that the conflict was a shameful war of conquest directed by a president bent on acquiring new territory for the likely expansion of slavery. Ulysses S. Grant, who fought in the war, later called it “one of the most unjust wars ever waged by a stronger against a weaker nation.”

The acquisition of the northern Mexican provinces made the United States a transcontinental nation and led to a dramatic expansion of the federal government. . . . Tensions between northern and southern leaders intensified as they battled over whether to support the war, and whether slavery should be extended to any of the new territories acquired from Mexico.

Word help: occupied = took control of · conquest = taking land by force · acquisition = getting · transcontinental = stretching across the continent · intensified = grew stronger

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 13, “The Mexican-American War” (The War’s Legacies) (p. 537).

Part 3 of 6

Slavery in the Territories

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 3: Describe how the federal government tried to resolve the issue of slavery in the western territories during the 1850s.

IN MY WORDS: How did Congress try to settle the fight over slavery in the West?

Reading GWilmot, Popular Sovereignty, and Free Soil

On August 8, 1846, only three months into the Mexican-American War, an obscure Democratic congressman from Pennsylvania, David Wilmot, delivered a speech to the House of Representatives in which he proposed that if any Mexican territory should be acquired, slavery would be banned there.

The Wilmot Proviso (1846) never became law; but by seeking to ban slavery in the newly acquired Mexican territories, it outraged pro-slavery legislators.

Senator Lewis Cass of Michigan suggested a different solution: that the citizens of each territory “regulate their own internal concerns in their own way” and decide for themselves whether slavery would be legal. . . . Popular sovereignty, as Cass called his idea, appealed to many who were eager to protect states’ rights.

As a result, keeping slavery out of the territories became the rallying cry for the Free-Soil Party, a new political organization that focused solely on stopping the spread of slavery.

Word help: obscure = not well known · proviso = a condition added to a law · sovereignty = the power to rule · rallying cry = a slogan that unites people

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 13, “Slavery in the Territories” (The Wilmot Proviso; Popular Sovereignty; The Free-Soil Movement) (p. 538). Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 13, “Reviewing the Core Objectives” (p. 568).

Reading HGold and the Compromise of 1850

In 1849, the California gold rush further escalated sectional tensions. Most Californians wanted their territory to become a free state. Southerners feared losing federal protection of slavery if free states outnumbered slave states.

In its final version, the Compromise of 1850 (see again Map 13.5) included five key elements:

(1) California entered the Union as a free state, ending forever the balance of free and slave states. . . . (3) The Utah Act set up the Utah Territory and gave the territorial legislature authority over “all rightful subjects of legislation,” including slavery. (4) A Fugitive Slave Act required the federal government and the northern states to help capture and return freedom seekers to the South. (5) As a gesture to anti-slavery groups, the slave trade, but not slavery itself, was abolished in the District of Columbia.

Word help: escalated = made bigger · sectional = between the North and the South · territorial legislature = lawmakers of a territory · freedom seekers = enslaved people who escaped · abolished = ended

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 13, “Reviewing the Core Objectives” (p. 568). Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 13, “Slavery in the Territories” (Compromise Efforts) (p. 544).

Reading IThe Fugitive Slave Act

The Fugitive Slave Act was the most controversial element of the Compromise of 1850. . . . The law even enabled slave-traders to kidnap free Blacks in northern “free” states, claiming that they were fugitive slaves; and it required citizens to help locate and capture any freedom seekers who had successfully escaped. . . . There was no jury, no testimony was allowed from the fugitives, and the commissioners themselves were paid $10 for returning runaways to slavery—but only $5 to free them.

Abolitionists fumed. Ralph Waldo Emerson urged people to break the new law. In New York, Reverend Jermain Loguen, himself a freedom seeker, shouted: “I don’t respect this law—I don’t fear it—I won’t obey it! It outlaws me, and I outlaw it.”

Word help: fugitive = someone running away · testimony = speaking in court · commissioners = officials who judged the cases · abolitionists = people who wanted to end slavery · fumed = were very angry

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 13, “Slavery in the Territories” (The Fugitive Slave Act) (p. 548).

Reading JThe Kansas-Nebraska Act

Unconcerned about the fate of Indigenous people, Douglas plowed ahead and urged Congress to pass the Kansas-Nebraska Act so that the vast northern territory west of Missouri and Iowa could be settled by Whites. To win the support of southern legislators, Douglas championed the principle of popular sovereignty, under which the voters themselves in each new western territory would decide whether to allow slavery. The legislation offered a way of getting around the 1820 Missouri Compromise, which excluded slavery north of the 36th parallel, where Kansas and Nebraska were located.

In 1854, Douglas and the Democrats pushed through the Kansas-Nebraska Act by a vote of 37–14 in the Senate and 113–100 in the House. The anti-slavery faction in Congress—mostly Whigs—had been crushed, and the national Whig Party died with them.

Word help: Douglas = Senator Stephen Douglas of Illinois · championed = strongly supported · excluded = kept out · 36th parallel = a line on the map; slavery was banned north of it · faction = group

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 13, “Slavery in the Territories” (The Kansas-Nebraska Crisis) (p. 552).

Part 4 of 6

The Rise of the Republican Party

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 4: Analyze the appeal of the Republican Party to northern voters and how it led to Abraham Lincoln's victory in the 1860 presidential contest.

IN MY WORDS: Why did more and more northern voters join the Republican Party?

Reading KBleeding Kansas and “Bleeding Sumner”

The passage of the Kansas-Nebraska Act soon placed Kansas at the center of the increasingly violent debate over slavery. . . . On Election Day, 5,000 “border ruffians” from Missouri crossed into Kansas. They seized polling places, illegally elected pro-slavery legislators (casting four times as many votes as there were residents) . . . The territorial legislature then declared the territory open to slavery.

Yet anti-slavery radicals could also be violent, such as John Brown in Bleeding Kansas (1856).

Southerners celebrated Brooks as a hero; dozens of supporters sent him new canes, one of which carried the inscription: “Hit Him Again.” In satisfying his rage, though, Brooks had created a martyr—“Bleeding Sumner”—for the anti-slavery cause. . . . Brooks’s assault on Sumner thus had an unintended political effect: it drove more northerners into the new Republican Party.

Word help: border ruffians = armed men from Missouri · polling places = where people vote · Brooks = a South Carolina congressman who beat Senator Charles Sumner with a cane · martyr = someone who suffers for a cause

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 13, “The Emergence of the Republican Party” (Bleeding Kansas; Violence in the Senate) (p. 555). Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 13, “Reviewing the Core Objectives” (p. 568).

MapMap 13.6: The Kansas-Nebraska Act, 1854

This modern textbook map shows free states, slave states, and the territories where voters could decide on slavery. The small map shows Bleeding Kansas.

Map key: Tan = free states and territories · Dark purple = slave states · Light purple = open to slavery by popular sovereignty, Compromise of 1850 · Green = open to slavery by popular sovereignty, Kansas-Nebraska Act · Red star = battle site

Norton, Ch. 13, Map 13.6, “The Kansas-Nebraska Act, 1854.” Modern textbook map.

Map evidence. (1) What color are Kansas and Nebraska Territories, and what does that color mean? (2) Are they north or south of the Missouri Compromise Line? (3) Why would that anger anti-slavery northerners?

Reading LThe Dred Scott Decision

The Supreme Court’s pro-slavery Dred Scott v. Sandford (1857) decision further fueled sectional conflict.

Chief Justice Roger B. Taney of Maryland, a devoted supporter of the South and of slavery, wrote the majority opinion. He ruled that Scott lacked legal standing because, like all enslaved people, he was property, not a human being. He was not a U.S. citizen and could never become one, nor was he eligible to file suit in a court.

The Dred Scott case directly challenged the concept of popular sovereignty. If Congress could not exclude slavery from a territory, as Taney argued, then neither could a territorial government created by an act of Congress. Suddenly, all the West—and the North—was open to slavery.

Word help: majority opinion = the ruling most judges agreed on · legal standing = the right to bring a case to court · file suit = sue in court · exclude = keep out

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 13, “Reviewing the Core Objectives” (p. 568). Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 13, “The Emergence of the Republican Party” (The Dred Scott Case) (p. 557).

Source PLincoln Debates Douglas, 1858 (Primary Source)

In 1858 Abraham Lincoln ran against Stephen Douglas for the U.S. Senate in Illinois. The seven Lincoln-Douglas debates drew thousands of people. Norton quotes Lincoln’s own words.

Douglas, he said, did not care whether slavery in the territories was “voted up, or voted down.” . . . “I have always hated slavery as much as any abolitionist,” he stressed. The American government, he predicted, could not “endure, permanently half slave and half free. . . . It will become all one thing or all the other.”

Word help: voted up, or voted down = allowed or banned by voters · stressed = said strongly · endure = last · permanently = forever

Abraham Lincoln, 1858, as quoted in Norton, Ch. 13, “The Emergence of the Republican Party” (Douglas versus Lincoln [1858]) (p. 560).

Source P. What did Lincoln say would happen to a nation that was half slave and half free?

Point of view. Lincoln was running for office against Douglas. Why would Lincoln say Douglas “did not care” about slavery? How might that help Lincoln win northern votes?

Reading MLincoln Wins in 1860

Although Lincoln won the popular vote, Douglas won the Senate seat because he had the support of the Democratic-controlled state legislature, which chose the winner. Lincoln’s energetic campaign, however, had made him a national figure.

The convention reaffirmed the party’s opposition to the extension of slavery and endorsed a series of traditional Whig policies promoting a higher protective tariff, free farms (homesteads) on federal lands in the West, and federally financed internal improvements, including a transcontinental railroad.

At midnight on November 6, Lincoln won with 39 percent of the popular vote, the smallest plurality ever, but he captured a clear majority (180 votes) in the Electoral College (see Map 13.7). He carried all eighteen free states but none of the slave states.

Word help: national figure = someone known across the country · reaffirmed = said again · protective tariff = a tax on imports that helps American factories · homesteads = free farms · plurality = the most votes, but not more than half

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 13, “The Emergence of the Republican Party” (Douglas versus Lincoln (1858); Lincoln’s Election (1860)) (p. 560).

Part 5 of 6

The South Leaves the Union

CORE OBJECTIVE

Core Objective 5: Explain why seven southern states seceded from the Union shortly after Lincoln's election in 1860.

IN MY WORDS: Why did southern states leave the Union after Lincoln won?

Reading NSecession

After Lincoln’s victory, South Carolina’s entire congressional delegation resigned. The state’s legislature then appointed a convention to decide whether it should secede from the Union. Nearly all the delegates owned enslaved people. Delegate Thomas Jefferson Withers declared that the “true question for us all is how shall we sustain African slavery in South Carolina from a series of annoying attacks?”

Meeting in Charleston on December 20, 1860, the special convention unanimously approved an Ordinance of Secession separating South Carolina from the United States.

By February 1, 1861, the other states of the Lower South—Florida, Georgia, Louisiana, and Texas—had also seceded. Although their secession ordinances mentioned various grievances against the federal government, they made clear that the primary reason for leaving the Union was their determination to preserve slavery.

Word help: delegation = group of representatives · secede = leave the Union · sustain = keep going · unanimously = with everyone agreeing · grievances = complaints · preserve = keep

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 13, “The Southern Response” (p. 565).

Reading OA President Who Did Nothing

Other southern states, especially those where the cotton economy reigned supreme, soon followed South Carolina’s lead in descending into disunion. The imploding nation desperately needed a bold, decisive president to intervene. Instead it suffered under the final weeks in office of James Buchanan, who blamed the crisis on fanatical abolitionists. He declared secession illegal, then claimed that he lacked the constitutional authority to stop it. “I can do nothing,” he sighed.

Before Lincoln was inaugurated, six other states joined South Carolina to form the Confederate States of America (CSA). South Carolinians bombarded Fort Sumter in Charleston Harbor, and so the Civil War began.

Word help: reigned supreme = was the most important · disunion = breaking up the country · fanatical = extreme · inaugurated = sworn in as president · bombarded = attacked with cannons

Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 13, “The Southern Response” (President Buchanan’s Waiting Game). Norton, America: The Essential Learning Edition, Ch. 13, “Reviewing the Core Objectives” (p. 568).
